extracted.intended_audience: reporters, copyreaders, proofreaders, newspaper editors, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for newspaper writing, punctuation, abbreviation, number usage, word division, titles, proofreading marks, and newsroom terminology aimed at producing and correcting newspaper copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound numbers between twenty and a hundred, when spelled out, should have a hyphen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word Division
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing a word at the end of a line, observe the following rules (numbered 1–9 and a general rule): do not break a syllable; do not divide a monosyllable; do not separate a consonant from a vowel that affects its pronunciation; do not divide a diphthong or separate two successive vowels one of which is silent; do not separate a syllable added by the addition of s; do not divide hyphenated words except at the regular hyphen; do not make awkward divisions; do not begin a line with a hyphen; as a rule, avoid dividing a word at the end of a line and never divide one at the end of a page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and anti-examples given: cre-ditable (correct), attempt-ed (wrong example shown as attempt-ed is incorrect), mob-bed, tho-ugh (do not divide monosyllables), nec-essity (wrong: ne-cessity), bo-wing and pe-ople given as incorrect divisions of bowing and people, financ-es (do not separate added s), pocket-book and fool-killer (hyphenated words may only be divided at the regular hyphen). Avoid awkward splits such as 'nothringy crack4e'. Never begin a line with a hyphen; never divide at end of page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations Avoided
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations should as a rule be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that the typewriter has created a tendency to write out all words in full; use abbreviations sparingly and only where prescribed by style rules below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal and Professional Titles (abbreviations before names)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following personal and professional titles are abbreviated when preceding proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List as given in the text: Adjt. Gen., Brig. Gen., Capt., Col., Dr., Gen., Gov., Gov. Gen., Hon., Lieut., Lieut. Col., Lieut. Gen., Maj., Maj. Gen., Mme., Mrs., Mr., M., Prof., Rev., Rt. Rev., Sergt., Supt., Mlle. (as printed in the source).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use personal titles under specified restrictions (rules 1–10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key rules: (1) Do not use Mr. before a man's name when his baptismal name or initials are given (example: use 'A. B. Crayton' not 'Mr. A. B. Crayton'); (2) After a person's name has been mentioned once in a story, omit initials/Christian names thereafter and put Mr. or professional title before the name (example: 'Prof. O. C. Bowen' then 'Prof. Bowen'); (3) If a person has more than one professional title, use the one of highest rank (or the one last received or best known if equal rank); (4) Mrs. always precedes the name of a married woman, Miss that of an unmarried woman; (5) In lists of unmarried women, precede names with 'Miss' giving the full Christian name of each; (6) In lists of married women, 'Mesdames' may introduce names though current usage prefers 'Mrs.' before each name; (7) When mentioning a man and his wife, write 'Mr. and Mrs. William Black' not 'William Black and wife'; (8) Do not use Master before the name of a boy; (9) Before 'Rev.' preceding the name of a clergyman always put 'the' (example: 'the Rev. T. P. Frost'); if initials are unknown write 'the Rev. Mr. Frost' not 'the Rev. Frost'. (10) (Implied) follow examples and demonstrated usages in the stylebook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of the Months (abbreviation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations of the months, except March, April, May, June, and July, are permissible when followed by a numeral indicating the day of the month, but not when used alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right: 'Richard Malone ... Sept. 18'; Wrong: 'the middle of Sept.' (when month used alone spell it out).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of the States (abbreviation rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of states, territories, and island possessions of the United States are abbreviated when preceded by the name of a town or city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miscellaneous Abbreviations (acceptable usages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain abbreviations are in good usage after proper names or when preceded by numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Esq., Inc., Jr., A.B., Ph.D., M.D., U.S.N.' after names; 'a.m., p.m., A.D., B.C.' when preceded by numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbidden Abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: The following abbreviations may not be used in most newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: (1) Christian names: Chas. for Charles, Thos. for Thomas; (2) Mount, Fort, and Saint: Mt., Ft., St. (e.g., 'Mt. St. Elias' or 'Ft. Wayne' forbidden as short forms); (3) Railroad, Company, Brothers, etc.: 'R. R.' for 'Railroad', 'Co.' for 'Company' (e.g., 'New Haven R. R.' and 'National Biscuit Co.' are not acceptable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dates (format rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules concerning how dates are written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1. Write year dates always in figures (example shown in source). 2. Write month dates in figures when preceded by the name of the month (example: 'July 7, 1916'). When the name of the month does not precede, spell out the date (example: 'Bills are due on the tenth'). 3. Do not write 'the 25th of December' — prefer 'Dec. 25.' 4. Do not put 'd^ nd, st, or th' after a date (example: write 'Sept. 7' not 'Sept. 7th').

rubrics_metrics.name: Money (numeric usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: When mentioning sums of money, use figures for all amounts over one dollar; spell out all sums below a dollar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '$5.75', 'fifty cents'. Exception: if in the same sentence amounts above and below a dollar appear, use figures for all amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Street and District Names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out street, ward, district, and precinct names designated by numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sporting Records (numeric usage)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: '10 feet, 5 inches'; 'Time, :40'; '18-2 balkline' (use figures for distances, times, scores).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning of Sentences (numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not begin a sentence with figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If impossible to shift the number later, place 'about' or 'more than' before the figures: example: 'More than 14,000 persons passed through the gates.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensions (format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use figures with an 'x' to express dimensions of lots, buildings, floors, boats, machinery, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Usage for Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: General rules concerning when to use figures versus spelled-out numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures to express dates, distances, latitude and longitude, hours of the day, degrees of temperature, percentage, street numbers, telephone numbers, automobile numbers, votes, and betting odds. In other cases spell out all numbers under 100, except where several numbers, some above and some under 100, are used in the same paragraph — then use figures for all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks for Correcting Copy (editorial shorthand)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of short editorial abbreviations and notations used by editors/copyreaders to indicate defects or instructions in copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List (as printed): amb - Ambiguous; and - A bad 'and' sentence. Make two sentences or subordinate one clause; ant - Antecedent not clear; Cl - Not clear; Cst - Construction faulty; Coh - Coherence not good; Con - Wrong connective; Consult - Bring copy to instructor for discussion; 8 - Delete; dull - Dull reading; E - Error; ed - Editorializing; too much personal opinion; FW - 'Fine writing.'; Gr - Bad grammar; K - Awkward; clumsily expressed; Id - Poor lead; revise; P - Punctuation wrong; pt - Point of view shifted; qt - Make this a direct quotation; rep - Same word repeated too much; rew - Rewrite; sent - Use shorter sentences; SI - Slang; Sp - Bad spelling; SU - Sentence lacks unity; T - Wrong tense; unnec - Unnecessary details; tr - Transpose; W - Wrong use of word; ? - Truth of statement questioned; If - Begin a new paragraph; No If - No If needed; _J - Indent; O - Put the words together as one; # - Separate into two words; * - Hyphen needed. (This list is to be used when marking corrections on copy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-Readers' Marks (typographical correction marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard proofreaders' marks and their meanings used when correcting printed proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List (as printed): Cap - Capitalize; lc - Lower case; S - Delete; stet - Restore the words crossed out; A (caret) - Insert at the place indicated; (period symbol) - Insert a period; A (comma symbol) - Insert a comma; ^ - Insert quotation-marks; '1' - Insert a hyphen; X - Imperfect letter; 9 - Letter inverted; ¶ (or similar) - Make a new paragraph; No ¶ - No paragraph; # - Put a space between; Nw^ - Smaller space; Close up; no space needed; Va - Badly spaced; space more evenly; ^_^ - Quad shows between the words; shove down; wf - Wrong font; tr - Transpose; r - Carry to the left; 11 - Lower; 1—1 - Elevate; / - Straighten crooked line; lead - Add lead between the lines; 8 lead - Take out lead; (?) - Query: Is the proof correct? (Note: the source includes typographic symbols; include the intended meaning when marking proofs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: newsroom glossary (definitions guiding production)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of newsroom terms that guide roles, tasks, and forms of copy used in newspaper production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selected entries and guidance included in the text: Ad Alley - part of composing room for advertisements; Add - late news added to a story; A.P. - Associated Press; Arrest Sheets - police record of arrests; Assignment - a story a reporter is detailed to cover; Assignment Slips - slips with daily assignments; Bank (Deck) - divisions of headlines or a table/frame for holding type-filled galleys; Bank-man - helper assembling type; Beat - regular place/section of town a reporter covers; B. F. - bold-face type; Blind Interview - interview where name is withheld; Blotter - police record-book of crime; Box - rectangular space to call attention to news; Break-line - a line not filled to the end with letters; Bridge - raised platform in police court; Bull - manifestly inconsistent statement(s); Bulldog Edition - earliest regular edition; Bulletin - brief telegraphic message with bare results; Catch-line - short line set in display type or a line at top of each page to help assembly; Chase - frame locking forms for printing; Condensed Type - thin type contrasted with extended type; Copy - any manuscript prepared for the press (with distinctions: Blind Copy, Clean Copy, Time Copy); Copy Cutter - assistant who cuts copy into takes for compositors; Copyholder - proof-reader's assistant who reads copy for comparison; Copy-reader - one who revises copy and writes headlines (distinct from proof-reader); Cover - to get facts about an event; Dead - composed type or copy of no further use; Deck - see Bank; Department Men - reporters assigned to same places; Display Type - bolder or more conspicuous type; Dope - information for a story; Em - unit of measurement for type; End Mark - mark at end of story (e.g., 30 in circle or #); Feature - to give prominence; Feature Story - human-interest story; Filler - story of doubtful news value included for lack of better news; Flash - brief telegraphic message inserted into running story; Flimsy - thin tissue paper for duplicating telegraphic stories; Flush - on an even line or margin; Follow Copy - instruction to follow copy exactly; Folo - abbreviation for follow to indicate stories to follow others; Form - assemblage of type locked in a chase; Fudge - small printing cylinder for late news; Future Book - record of future events for reporters; Galley - tray for holding composed type; Galley Proof - impression pulled from galley; Gothic - heavy black-faced type; Guide Line - see Catch Line; Hanging Indention - indention style; Head - abbreviation for headline; Hell-box - box for waste lead; Hold - instruction to hold an article from printing; Human Interest Story - see Feature Story; I.N.S. - International News Service; Insert - sentences/paragraphs inserted in a body of story; Jump-head - headline above continuation of story; Justifier - short story of little news value; Justify - to make even by spacing; Kill - to destroy whole or part of a story; Lead - initial sentence/paragraph cramming the gist of the article (also thin metal strips called leads used in typesetting); Lower Case - definition and origin; Make-up - arrangement of type into columns/pages; Make-up Man - worker arranging composed type; Morgue - filing cabinet/room with stored stories and materials; Must - direction meaning story must be printed; Pi - jumbled/disarranged type; Pi Line - a freak line set up by an error; Play Up - to emphasize by writing about with fullness; Police Blotter - see Blotter; Pony Report - condensed report of day's news sent to smaller papers; Proof-reader - one who reads and makes corrections in printer's proof (distinct from copy-reader); Prove - to take a proof of or from; Pull - to make an impression on a hand-press; Pyramid Head - multi-line heading with indention pattern; Query - telegraphic request for instructions on a story; Quoins - wedges used for locking type; Release - permit publication on or after a specified date; Revise - a corrected proof; Rewrite - story rewritten from another paper; Rewrite Man - reporter who rewrites telegraphic/poor copy; Run - see Beat; Run-in - omit paragraph indentions to save space; Running Story - story developing as day advances; Scoop - publication of important story in advance of rivals; Sheets - see Arrest Sheets; Slips - short announcements pasted/clipped; Slug - various meanings relating to typographic slug or the linotype operator; Solid - having no leads between lines; Space Book - record of stories sent by correspondents; Space Writer - paid by amount of printed space; Special - story by a special correspondent; Stick - small metal tray or amount of type; Stone - table for page forms; Story - any article other than editorial/advertisement; Streamer Head - head extending across page; String - strip of clipped stories indicating column contribution; Style Book - printed book of rules followed by reporters/copyreaders/compositors (this work); Take - portion of copy taken by a compositor; '80' - telegrapher's end-of-message signal; Tip - secret information valuable to a paper; Turn Rule - signal to composing room to indicate more is to come; U.P. - United Press Associations; W.f. - wrong font (proof-reader's mark).
